1 — “Visible only from the air” is incorrect

Nazca research increasingly emphasises ground-level routes, hills and paths. Ruggles and Saunders's field-based study showed that some line systems could be experienced as a ceremonial “labyrinth” when followed on foot.
The Yamagata University and IBM Research team verified 303 new figurative geoglyphs. Most large
figures depict wild animals and are associated with networks of linear/trapezoidal ceremonial features. Smaller
figures more often show motifs connected with human activities, such as people, domesticated camelids and severed heads; these tend to lie near winding paths.

4 — The water connection is appealing, but not the only explanation

In an arid environment, water was central to Nasca society's rituals and settlement patterns. Some lines have been linked to water sources, valleys or groundwater systems. But there is insufficient evidence to explain every geoglyph as a “groundwater map”.

Astronomical calendars, ritual walking, water and sacred-landscape theories are extensively debated.
The Nasca and Palpa lines enter the UNESCO World Heritage List.
New dating and ground-level landscape studies further weaken single-purpose explanations.
AI-assisted surveying verifies 303 new figurative geoglyphs and strengthens two different models of use.
Theory A — Ritual routes and community ceremonies

Field studies show connections between lines, trapezoids, some figures, linked sacred places and walking routes. The 2024 PNAS findings strengthen the idea of community-scale use, particularly for large line-type figures.
“Ritual” is a broad category; it does not tell us exactly which ceremony used each line.
Theory B — An astronomical calendar / celestial alignments
Some lines may have meaningful solar or celestial orientations, and the ritual importance of celestial events in Andean societies is known.
In an enormous dataset of thousands of lines, chance alignments are inevitable. There is no strong evidence reducing the whole system to a single celestial calendar.
Theory C — Water worship, fertility and sacred landscape
Water was vital in Nazca's extremely arid environment; the Andean world contains strong connections between water sources, mountains and rituals.
It has not been shown that every geoglyph corresponds to groundwater or an irrigation system.
Theory D — Route markers and social information
The clustering of small relief-type figures near winding paths, with motifs related to human activities, supports this interpretation in the 2024 study.
Which motif conveyed which message remains unresolved.
Theory E — There was no single purpose
Different periods, techniques, scales, motifs and spatial contexts show why there is no need to expect a single function over hundreds of years.
Even if a multifunctional model is correct, explaining the exact meaning of individual lines remains difficult.
“They can only be seen from an aircraft.”
Some can be perceived from nearby hills and at ground level; some are already associated with paths and walking routes.
The archaeological context, techniques and motifs are consistent with local Paracas/Nasca cultures. The “runway” interpretation is not based on physical evidence.
“The Nazca people could not have made lines this straight.”
Straight lines and large figures can be produced using simple stakes, ropes and measuring techniques; extraordinary technology is not required.
Some alignments may exist, but modern research gives greater weight to models of multiple ritual and social uses.
Water is an important context, but there is insufficient evidence to explain every line as part of a single hydraulic map.
AI accelerated the identification of candidates; field teams verified them. The study supplied strong new patterns concerning function, but not a “final solution”.
We do not know for certain why monkeys, spiders, birds and other motifs were chosen.
Some may have been ceremonial routes, others social markers, and others may have served astronomical or environmental functions.
Thinking that a feature was walked along or used ceremonially is different from knowing exactly what the ritual involved.
For each group, we do not know who planned the work, how many people participated, or which social authority managed the projects.
The 2024 study points to information transfer in the figures' distribution, but this symbolic system has not yet been read.
Not every geoglyph has been directly dated. Even where the general period is known, the ages of individual features often depend on contextual inference.
🟡 The mystery is becoming clearer — but expecting “one answer” is probably misguided from the outset.

The strongest shift in Nazca research is that researchers are moving away from treating the lines as a giant riddle with the question “What was their single purpose?” The same region contains numerous geoglyphs made over hundreds of years using different techniques in different social contexts.
My most likely interpretation is therefore:
the Nazca landscape was a multilayered cultural system combining ritual walks, community ceremonies, social information, water and relationships with sacred geography.
Some lines may have had astronomical functions, but that does not explain the entire system.
The most remarkable question is not “How did they make them?” They could do that using simple tools. It is
what world of meaning this vast landscape created for them.
The basic context of production and use is increasingly understood; symbolic meanings and the purposes of individual features remain open.
